paragraphs: The paper studies neural operators through an optimization perspective. It treats the action of an operator layer as the solution to a Bregman-regularized optimization problem over a space of functions. This gives the layer a mathematical interpretation in terms of what it minimizes, connecting its computation to the geometry used by that optimization problem.

Within this framework, activation operators become Bregman proximity operators that map from a dual space back to a primal space. The framework covers classical neural operators and also leads to a new family called Bregman neural operators. These incorporate the inverse activation operator while retaining the same expressivity as standard neural operators.

The authors test a Bregman version of Fourier neural operators numerically. Their experiments support benefits for training deeper models and obtaining greater accuracy. The contribution therefore combines a broader mathematical description of existing architectures with a concrete architectural variant. The stated advantage concerns training and observed accuracy, while expressive capacity remains equivalent to that of the standard operators.
icml-2025-a-bregman-proximal-viewpoint-o.tldr: An optimization-based interpretation of neural operators leads to a Bregman variant with equal expressivity and experimentally supported benefits for depth and accuracy.

paragraphs: Zero-shot prediction uses representations learned before a particular downstream task is specified, then applies them to that task without labeled examples for it. The paper examines this foundation-model paradigm theoretically, focusing on models generally obtained through self-supervised learning and contrastive learning across multiple kinds of data.

The framework identifies the target quantities involved in zero-shot prediction. It distinguishes quantities the learning procedure seeks directly from those it learns along the way. This distinction matters because the information acquired during pretraining must support a later prediction problem, even though that problem supplies no labeled training data of its own.

The authors also identify conditional independence relationships that enable generalization. These relationships describe which dependencies between variables remain relevant once other information is known. Together, the target quantities and independence structure provide a way to reason about how pretrained representations can support unseen prediction tasks. The contribution is an account of the statistical structure enabling this transfer, rather than a new reported benchmark result or a claim that every pretrained model generalizes successfully.
icml-2025-a-generalization-theory-for-ze.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework identifying what zero-shot prediction learns and the conditional independence relationships that enable generalization.

paragraphs: The paper brings anytime constraints into Markov games, where multiple players make decisions as a system evolves. Such constraints concern feasibility throughout the process. The authors introduce an associated solution concept, an anytime-constrained equilibrium, to describe strategic behavior under these requirements.

Their theory addresses both whether a policy is feasible and how an equilibrium can be computed. It includes a computational characterization of feasible policies, a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for computing these equilibria, and a polynomial-time algorithm for approximate computation. These results provide different routes to computation, depending on whether one uses the parameterized formulation or accepts approximation.

The difficulty is substantial: even finding a feasible policy is NP-hard for two-player zero-sum games. The authors show that their approximation guarantees are the best possible under the assumption that P differs from NP. They also develop a theory of efficient computation for action-constrained Markov games. Together, the results clarify both the algorithms available for constrained strategic decision-making and the complexity barriers that shape their guarantees.
icml-2025-anytime-constrained-equilibria.tldr: The paper defines anytime-constrained equilibria and gives computation and approximation algorithms with guarantees that are optimal assuming P differs from NP.

paragraphs: Many optimization algorithms change their update rule during a run, for example by adjusting a step size, momentum parameter, or Hessian approximation. When such an algorithm solves the inner problem of a bilevel optimization task, an outer objective may require gradients through that entire sequence of updates.

The paper analyzes what happens when automatic differentiation is applied to these time-varying iterative processes. Unrolling the solver produces a sequence of derivative estimates alongside its ordinary optimization iterates. The authors provide guarantees for convergence of those derivatives, including rates, so the analysis concerns how reliably differentiation through repeated updates approaches its limiting result.

They specialize the results to proximal gradient descent with varying step sizes and to FISTA on partly-smooth problems. Numerical experiments examine the predicted convergence behavior. Across the theoretical and numerical results, the optimization algorithm's convergence rate is reflected in its derivative iterates. This connects solver behavior to the behavior of the gradients used by an outer optimization problem, within the settings covered by the analysis.
icml-2025-automatic-differentiation-of-o.tldr: The paper establishes convergence rates for differentiating through time-varying optimization algorithms and connects derivative convergence to the solver's own convergence.

paragraphs: Comparing reinforcement learning methods requires deciding what counts as better performance and whether an observed difference is statistically convincing. The paper addresses this measurement problem, which becomes especially important when evaluating claims that quantum reinforcement learning offers an advantage over other approaches.

The authors propose a benchmarking methodology built around a statistical estimator of sample complexity and a definition of statistical outperformance. This gives comparisons an explicit basis in the amount of experience needed and in statistical evidence for superiority. They apply the methodology in a new benchmarking environment whose complexity can be varied, allowing performance to be examined across different levels of task difficulty.

The resulting findings cast doubt on some earlier claims of quantum reinforcement learning superiority. They still identify possible advantages, but the overall conclusions are more qualified. The paper also discusses limitations of its results and implications for empirical research on quantum advantage. Its contribution is both a comparison procedure and evidence that conclusions about quantum benefits depend on careful statistical validation.
icml-2025-benchmarking-quantum-reinforce.tldr: A statistical benchmarking methodology yields a more qualified assessment of quantum reinforcement learning advantages and challenges some earlier superiority claims.

paragraphs: Decoder-only models retain key and value vectors while generating tokens, and the growing cache can make inference limited by memory. CLOVER addresses this by pruning attention components through a representation that exposes linear redundancy within individual attention heads.

The method treats query-key and value-output component pairs as low-rank decompositions and applies singular value decomposition to them. The resulting singular values determine what to prune. They also become trainable parameters during efficient fine-tuning, allowing recovery of pre-pruning performance. Afterward, those values are folded back into the model without increasing its parameter count.

The reported results illustrate how this representation changes pruning efficiency. In GPT-2 XL, removing 70% of the query-key head dimension gives perplexity comparable to removing only 8% with vanilla pruning. Separately, combining CLOVER with TransMLA produces a speedup of up to 11.1 times over LLaMA-2-7B. These examples support the value of identifying redundant directions before pruning; the speedup is specifically a result for the combined method, rather than CLOVER alone.
icml-2025-clover-cross-layer-orthogonal-.tldr: CLOVER uses singular value decomposition to prune redundant attention dimensions and efficiently fine-tune the remaining representation.

paragraphs: DiMA generates protein sequences by applying continuous diffusion to representations produced by protein language models. This places generation in an encoded space, extending protein design approaches that operate through discrete diffusion or autoregressive sequence generation.

The authors systematically explore architectural and diffusion choices and develop one architecture and training approach that works across several representation types. The tested encoders range from 8 million to 3 billion parameters and include sequence-only, dual-decodable, and multimodal representations. This breadth matters because the framework can be used with substantially different protein encodings while preserving its overall design.

Evaluation examines quality, diversity, novelty, and distribution matching across two protein modalities. DiMA produces novel, diverse, high-quality sequences and reports strong results against autoregressive, discrete diffusion, and flow-matching language models. It also supports protein-family generation, motif scaffolding, infilling, and fold-specific sequence design despite training solely on sequence data. The findings position continuous diffusion over language-model encodings as a flexible approach to several protein sequence design tasks.
icml-2025-diffusion-on-language-model-en.tldr: DiMA applies continuous diffusion to protein language-model representations, generating diverse sequences and supporting multiple conditional design tasks.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a mathematical framework that represents data classes as vectors. Within this construction, vector addition corresponds to class union, while scalar multiplication resembles taking class complements. The authors identify the zero vector with a particular class they call the Metta-Class and use it to develop several learning applications.

One application, called clear learning, aims to learn the data manifold—the structure occupied by the data—rather than only a boundary sufficient for classification. Another, unary class learning, learns a class in isolation instead of through comparison with other classes. The framework also supports set operations on classes and is presented as facilitating continual learning with smaller networks.

The authors connect learning the manifold through the Metta-Class to generating new data. They show results for the main applications on MNIST and provide additional results using CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k embeddings. The contribution combines a proposed algebraic view of classes with demonstrations of the learning behaviors it enables in these settings.
icml-2025-discovering-a-zero-zero-vector.tldr: The paper introduces a vector-space framework for classes whose Metta-Class supports manifold learning, isolated class learning, and other demonstrated applications.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many measurements are needed to recover a binary vector exactly when only k of its n entries are nonzero. It considers generalized linear measurements, including logistic regression and noisy measurements reduced to a single bit. The authors analyze a linear estimation algorithm and derive information-theoretic lower bounds.

For noisy one-bit measurements, linear estimation needs O((k + σ²) log n) samples, where σ² is the noise variance. A matching lower bound establishes optimality of this sample complexity. The paper also gives a tight characterization for logistic regression. Because one-bit quantization makes the measurement problem harder, the same achievable sample complexity carries over to noisy linear measurements, with linear estimation offering greater computational efficiency than lasso.

For noisy linear measurements, the lower bound applies to arbitrary measurement sets and is closely matched by a maximum-likelihood upper bound. The authors also establish that there is no statistical-computational gap in the one-bit and logistic settings considered. That conclusion specifically concerns those settings, alongside a discussion of a conjectured gap for sparse linear regression.
icml-2025-exact-recovery-of-sparse-binar.tldr: Linear estimation achieves optimal sample complexity for exact sparse binary recovery from noisy one-bit measurements, with tight results also obtained for logistic regression.

paragraphs: Estimating how treatment effects differ between people becomes difficult when the outcome is time until an event. Right-censoring means that some event times remain unobserved, and treating these records as fully observed can cause bias and inefficiency. The paper focuses particularly on heavy censoring, where an existing doubly-robust survival method struggles.

The proposed method, Multiple Imputation for Survival Treatment Response, or MISTR, uses recursively imputed survival trees. It handles censoring without directly modeling the censoring mechanism and provides a general, non-parametric approach to heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation. The method also extends to instrumental variables, addressing a setting that many existing approaches cannot handle.

Simulations and analyses of the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Protocol 175 and Illinois unemployment datasets support the approach. Under heavy censoring and no hidden confounders, MISTR outperforms prior methods. Its instrumental-variable extension also covers unobserved confounding. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first non-parametric method for this survival treatment-effect problem using instrumental variables.
icml-2025-heterogeneous-treatment-effect.tldr: MISTR uses recursively imputed survival trees to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects under censoring and extends to instrumental-variable settings.

paragraphs: Residual connections are central architectural components in both vision networks and transformer language models. The paper introduces the Learned Augmented Residual Layer, or LAuReL, as a generalization that can replace the conventional residual connection in place. Its aim is to improve model quality with a small increase in model footprint.

Experiments cover both vision and language tasks. The authors find that LAuReL can improve quality while requiring fewer additional parameters and less latency and memory overhead than simply increasing parameter count. On ImageNet-1K, it matches the quality improvement from adding another layer while using 2.6 times fewer parameters for that improvement.

In pretraining experiments with 1-billion- and 4-billion-parameter language models, LAuReL improves performance on various challenging downstream tasks by 2.54% to 20.05%. The respective parameter additions are only 0.012% and 0.1%. These results support modifying residual connections as an efficient architectural route to better performance, with the reported improvements tied to the tested models and evaluations.
icml-2025-laurel-learned-augmented-resid.tldr: LAuReL replaces standard residual connections with a learned generalization that improves tested vision and language models with very small parameter overhead.

paragraphs: Different decision trees can describe exactly the same decision boundary while following different sequences of tests. The paper calls this predictive equivalence. It creates a selection problem because equivalent trees can assign different importance to variables and behave differently when feature values are missing, even though their boundaries agree.

The authors introduce a Boolean logical representation that stays faithful to the decision boundary without exhibiting this equivalence problem. This separates the underlying prediction rule from the particular tree structure chosen to evaluate it. That distinction matters when an optimization procedure would otherwise return one of several equivalent trees arbitrarily.

The paper applies the representation to missing features, variable importance, and evaluation cost. It shows that decision trees can be surprisingly robust to missing feature values at test time, addresses how predictive equivalence affects importance measurements, and provides an algorithm for optimizing the cost of reaching predictions. Together, these applications show why understanding the shared decision boundary can improve how equivalent tree models are interpreted and used.
icml-2025-leveraging-predictive-equivale.tldr: A Boolean representation of decision boundaries resolves predictive equivalence in trees and supports better analysis of missing values, variable importance, and prediction cost.

paragraphs: Loss-to-loss scaling laws describe relationships between a language model's losses on different pretraining datasets and downstream tasks. They offer a way to understand how progress measured in one setting relates to performance elsewhere. This paper investigates which choices in model development most strongly determine those relationships.

The experiments identify pretraining data as the factor determining the scaling trend. Model size, optimization hyperparameters, and tokenizer choices generally have limited influence on that trend. The same pattern extends to substantial architectural differences, including the comparison between transformer models such as Llama and state-space models such as Mamba.

The practical implication is that dataset curation deserves particular attention when targeting downstream performance. The findings also suggest room to choose architectures and training settings for efficiency while maintaining similar loss-to-loss relationships. This is an empirical conclusion about the scaling trends examined: it does not say that architecture or optimization choices have no effect on training. It identifies data as the dominant influence on how losses relate across settings.
icml-2025-llms-on-the-line-data-determin.tldr: Experiments find that pretraining data determines loss-to-loss scaling trends, while architecture and other training choices generally have limited influence.

paragraphs: LOCATE 3D locates objects in three-dimensional scenes from language descriptions that can specify appearance and spatial relationships. It works directly with posed RGB-D sensor frames, making its input compatible with observations available to robots and augmented-reality devices.

Its core learning method, 3D-JEPA, starts from a point cloud enriched with features from the two-dimensional foundation models CLIP and DINO. It learns contextual point-cloud features through masked prediction in a latent representation. The trained encoder is then fine-tuned together with a language-conditioned decoder to predict both three-dimensional object masks and bounding boxes.

The authors also introduce a referential-grounding dataset containing over 130,000 annotations from multiple capture setups. This supports both a stronger model and systematic evaluation of generalization across setups. LOCATE 3D achieves state-of-the-art results on standard referential-grounding benchmarks and demonstrates robust generalization. The contribution connects self-supervised learning of three-dimensional context with language-guided localization and a sensor-based input format suited to real-world deployment.
icml-2025-locate-3d-real-world-object-lo.tldr: LOCATE 3D combines self-supervised point-cloud learning with language-conditioned decoding to locate objects directly from RGB-D sensor observations.

paragraphs: Evolutionary model merging searches for combinations of existing language models that perform well across tasks. Evaluating candidate merges can make this search too expensive for consumer hardware. MERGE³ targets that evaluation burden so evolutionary merging can run on a single GPU.

The framework has three connected components. It extracts a smaller evaluation dataset, estimates model abilities through Item Response Theory, and uses those performance estimates to guide the evolution of candidate merges. The central idea is to make fitness computation cheaper while retaining useful information about which merges are promising.

The authors report a 50-fold reduction in fitness computation costs while preserving a large fraction of the original performance. They also report state-of-the-art multilingual and cross-lingual merging, with knowledge transferred across languages at substantially lower computational overhead. The work includes theoretical guarantees and an open-source library. Its efficiency claim specifically concerns fitness evaluation, and the retained performance is described as a large fraction rather than complete preservation of the original results.
icml-2025-merge-3-efficient-evolutionary.tldr: MERGE³ uses reduced evaluation data and Item Response Theory to cut evolutionary merging fitness costs 50-fold and enable single-GPU operation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how efficiently optimal policies can be approximated in constrained Markov decision processes. These problems require balancing a policy's objective with restrictions on its behavior, and the computational difficulty can depend strongly on how those restrictions are expressed.

The main result is a polynomial-time algorithm with a (0, ε) additive bicriteria guarantee. Its framework covers a broad family of recursively computable constraints, including almost-sure, chance, expectation, and anytime forms. Using a common formulation allows the authors to address multiple constraint types within one approximation approach.

The results settle several open questions about polynomial-time approximability. They cover policies under chance constraints, deterministic policies with multiple expectation constraints, policies facing a mixture of constraint types, and constrained policies in continuous-state processes. Matching lower bounds show that the approximation guarantees are optimal if P differs from NP. The significance is therefore both constructive and limiting: the paper supplies efficient approximation algorithms while establishing why stronger guarantees cannot generally be expected under that complexity assumption.
icml-2025-polynomial-time-approximabilit.tldr: A polynomial-time approximation framework covers broad constrained decision problems with guarantees that matching lower bounds show are optimal if P differs from NP.

paragraphs: Computing a Nash equilibrium in a normal-form game is difficult, motivating approaches that turn equilibrium approximation into a non-convex optimization problem. When these methods use sampled play, the choice of loss function affects both what is estimated and how noisy that estimate becomes.

The paper identifies high variance in the existing unbiased loss as a barrier to convergence. It introduces Nash Advantage Loss, or NAL, as a surrogate designed to reduce that variance while preserving unbiasedness. The authors theoretically establish that NAL is unbiased and has significantly lower variance than the previous unbiased loss.

Experiments show that minimizing NAL converges substantially faster than the compared algorithms and reduces variance in estimated loss values by several orders of magnitude. These results connect a statistical property of the optimization objective to practical progress toward an approximate equilibrium. The contribution improves the loss used by stochastic optimization; the stated empirical speed advantage concerns the tested algorithms and games, while the unbiasedness and variance results receive theoretical support.
icml-2025-reducing-variance-of-stochasti.tldr: Nash Advantage Loss preserves unbiased estimation while reducing variance, yielding substantially faster empirical convergence when approximating Nash equilibria.

paragraphs: Conditional value at risk, or CVaR, focuses policy optimization on the poor-return part of the outcome distribution. Existing policy-gradient methods for this objective discard a large share of collected trajectories. The paper identifies this loss of usable training experience as a cause of poor sample efficiency.

The proposed reformulation caps the total return assigned to trajectories used in training instead of simply throwing those trajectories away. This changes how collected experience enters the optimization problem. The authors show that the reformulated problem is equivalent to the original CVaR problem when the cap is chosen appropriately, so that choice is central to the equivalence claim.

Across experiments in several environments, return capping consistently improves performance relative to the tested baselines. The results support retaining trajectories through a suitable transformation of their returns as a way to improve CVaR policy-gradient training. The contribution combines a conditional theoretical equivalence with empirical evidence that this reformulation makes better use of the experience collected during learning.
icml-2025-return-capping-sample-efficien.tldr: Capping trajectory returns yields an equivalent CVaR optimization problem when the cap is appropriate and improves performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Scaling laws help predict how language-model performance changes as training grows and guide configuration choices that would otherwise require expensive experimentation. This paper addresses those questions when training must protect sensitive data through differential privacy, a setting whose training dynamics differ substantially from ordinary language-model training.

The authors establish scaling laws designed to capture the specific behavior of differentially private language models. Their formulation describes the relationship between computation, privacy, and utility. Treating these quantities together matters because a useful training configuration must account for the privacy requirement alongside the available computational resources and desired model performance.

The resulting laws accurately model the intricacies of private training and identify optimal configurations in many settings. Their practical role is to support training decisions with predictions that reflect privacy-preserving training itself. The contribution extends the planning value of scaling laws to a setting where relying on the dynamics of ordinary training would leave an essential part of the compute and performance relationship unaccounted for.
icml-2025-scaling-laws-for-differentiall.tldr: The paper develops scaling laws for differentially private language models that characterize compute, privacy, and utility trade-offs and guide training configurations.

paragraphs: Signal temporal logic specifies tasks with logical and timing requirements. Learning to solve diverse specifications is difficult when training data and representations cover mainly fixed or narrowly parameterized forms. TeLoGraF addresses this with a graph neural network encoder and flow matching for learning solutions to general temporal-logic specifications.

The authors identify four commonly used specification templates and assemble 200,000 specifications paired with demonstrations. The graph encoder extracts information from the logical structure, while flow matching forms part of the learned solution method. Evaluation spans five simulated environments, from two-dimensional dynamical systems to a seven-degree-of-freedom Franka Panda arm and Ant quadruped navigation.

TeLoGraF achieves higher specification-satisfaction rates than the tested baselines. Compared with classical temporal-logic planners, it reports inference that is 10 to 100 times faster, and the approach is presented as applicable to any system dynamics. Further results demonstrate the graph encoding's ability to handle complex specifications and robustness to specifications outside the training distribution. These findings support learning across a broader range of logically structured tasks.
icml-2025-telograf-temporal-logic-planni.tldr: TeLoGraF combines graph encoding and flow matching to solve diverse temporal-logic tasks, improving tested satisfaction rates and speeding inference relative to classical planners.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether released synthetic text can reveal information about the data used to fine-tune its generating language model. It assumes an adversary has access to some generated data and constructs membership inference attacks targeting the fine-tuning records. The attacks' performance shows that synthetic text can carry information about those records.

The authors also examine canaries used to audit privacy leakage. Canaries designed for attacks with model access work poorly when only synthetic data is released. If a canary is far outside the normal data distribution, prompts requesting useful, in-distribution text give it little influence on generated outputs, reducing its detectability.

The proposed canaries combine a prefix that fits the data distribution with a high-perplexity suffix. This construction uses the mechanics of autoregressive generation to leave detectable traces in synthetic text. It strengthens membership inference based on released data and improves privacy auditing for this release scenario. The findings show why an audit must account for the generation pipeline and the information an adversary actually receives.
icml-2025-the-canarys-echo-auditing-priv.tldr: Synthetic text can expose fine-tuning membership, and canaries tailored to the generation process improve detection of that privacy leakage.

paragraphs: Parallel reinforcement learning actors can gather experience from many environments at once, but the way that experience is collected changes learning behavior. This paper examines those choices empirically in PPO, focusing on the number of parallel environments, rollout length, and repeated training passes over the collected data.

Environment count and rollout length induce a bias-variance trade-off. Reusing a collected dataset creates a separate balance between sample efficiency and overfitting. The authors connect these decisions to network plasticity, meaning its ability to keep adapting, and to optimization stability. They also examine how architecture and sensitivity to hyperparameters interact with larger data collections.

The analyses indicate that larger datasets can improve final performance across a variety of settings. Increasing the number of parallel environments is more effective than extending rollout lengths in the reported comparisons. The findings make data collection a substantive part of algorithm design: both the amount of experience and how that experience is distributed across parallel environments and time affect learning outcomes.
icml-2025-the-impact-of-on-policy-parall.tldr: PPO experiments indicate that larger datasets can improve performance and that adding parallel environments is more effective than lengthening rollouts.

paragraphs: A generated video can depict a complex prompt while still violating basic physical expectations. The paper investigates this gap through PhyGenBench, a benchmark designed to assess physical commonsense in text-to-video generation. It contains 160 carefully designed prompts covering 27 physical laws across four domains.

The accompanying evaluation framework, PhyGenEval, uses a hierarchical structure involving vision-language models and language models to judge physical correctness. This supports large-scale automated assessment, with judgments that closely align with human feedback. The combination provides both a set of physical challenges and a way to evaluate generated videos against them.

The authors find that the evaluated models struggle to produce videos consistent with physical commonsense. Increasing model scale or applying prompt engineering does not fully resolve the benchmark's challenges, including dynamic scenarios. These results distinguish the ability to visualize a prompt from the ability to represent its physical behavior reliably. The benchmark is intended to direct attention toward physical understanding as video generation develops toward world simulation.
icml-2025-towards-world-simulator-crafti.tldr: PhyGenBench and PhyGenEval reveal persistent physical-commonsense failures in tested video generators that scaling and prompt engineering do not fully resolve.

paragraphs: The paper studies access to a matrix through a restricted kind of query: multiplying it by a vector assembled as a Kronecker product of smaller vectors. It asks how this structure affects the number of queries needed to learn matrix properties such as the trace or largest eigenvalue.

The authors prove exponential query lower bounds for these estimation tasks. The results cover adaptive algorithms, whose later queries depend on earlier answers, subject to a mild conditioning assumption on the queries. They also show that queries whose component vectors use a small alphabet, such as entries restricted to plus or minus one, cannot test whether the matrix is zero with polynomial query complexity.

In contrast, a single query using Gaussian vectors resolves that zero-matrix test with probability one. Thus, distributions with the same subgaussian norm can have exponentially different query complexity in the Kronecker setting. The proofs connect this separation to the exponentially smaller inner products of random Kronecker-structured vectors compared with their unstructured counterparts.
icml-2025-understanding-the-kronecker-ma.tldr: Kronecker-structured matrix queries face exponential complexity barriers, and changing the query distribution can produce exponentially different performance.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization occurs when a student trained on a weaker teacher's labels performs better than that teacher. The paper proves that this can happen in simple, non-pretrained random-feature networks. In these two-layer models, the bottom layer remains randomly fixed while the top layer is trained.

The teacher has relatively few features and is trained on the population. A much larger student then learns only from teacher-generated labels. The authors demonstrate and explain how the student's size advantage can produce better performance despite that restricted supervision. They also identify early stopping as a mechanism enabling the improvement.

The paper establishes quantitative limits that extend beyond the specific random-feature setup to arbitrary teacher and student feature spaces and a broad class of learning rules. These limits also cover pretrained or otherwise more informative student features. Within the covered models, student error can approach zero only if teacher error does, and a teacher that is only slightly better than chance cannot be boosted into a low-error student. The results establish both a simple mechanism for improvement and a boundary on its extent.
icml-2025-weak-to-strong-generalization-.tldr: Larger random-feature students can outperform their teachers through early stopping, but provable limits prevent arbitrarily strong improvement from weak supervision.
